u.src: The tale tells how Tripitaka and his disciples broke through the web of desire, escaped the prison of passion, and set their horse westward.
Before they had gone far, summer ended and autumn began, and a fresh coolness pierced their bodies.
This is what they saw:

p.src: As Tripitaka journeyed on, he suddenly saw a lofty mountain whose peaks pierced the blue vault, truly scraping the stars and blocking the sun. The elder grew afraid and called to Wukong, “Look how exceedingly high and steep that mountain ahead is. I wonder whether there is a road through it.” Pilgrim laughed. “What are you saying, Master? As the old proverb goes, ‘However high the mountain, travelers find a road; however deep the water, ferrymen will be there.’ How could there be no way through? Set your mind at ease and go on.” Hearing this, the elder’s face blossomed into a joyful smile. He raised his whip, urged his horse onward, and went straight up the lofty crags.

p.src: After traveling only a few miles, they saw an old man with tousled temples and fluttering white hair; his sparse beard swayed in silvery strands; a string of prayer beads hung around his neck, and in his hand he held a dragon-headed staff. Standing far off on the mountainside, he called loudly, “Elder traveling west, rein in your fine steed a while and draw the jade bridle tight! A band of fiends lives on this mountain. They have devoured all the people of Jambudvipa. You must go no farther.” At these words, Tripitaka turned pale with alarm. The footing beneath the horse was uneven, and he himself sat unsteadily in the carved saddle; with a thud he tumbled from the horse, lay helpless in the grass, and groaned. Pilgrim stepped forward and helped him up, saying, “Don’t be afraid, don’t be afraid. I am here.” The elder said, “You heard that old man on the high crag warn us that a band of fiends on this mountain has devoured all the people of Jambudvipa. Who dares go and ask him the true particulars?” Pilgrim said, “Sit here for now and let me go question him.” Tripitaka said, “Your features are ugly and your speech uncouth. I fear you may offend him and fail to learn the truth.” Pilgrim laughed. “I’ll change into someone more handsome before I ask him.” Tripitaka said, “Then transform yourself and let me see.” Dear Great Sage! He formed a spell with his fingers, shook himself, and changed into a neat and tidy young monk, truly with bright eyes, fine brows, a round head, and a well-formed face; his every movement bore an air of refinement, and no vulgar expression passed his lips. He shook out his brocade robe, strode forward, and asked the Tang Monk, “Master, do you think I have transformed well?” Tripitaka was delighted at the sight and said, “Very well indeed.” Bajie said, “How could it not be good? The only trouble is that he makes all of us look inferior. Even if old Pig rolled about for two or three years, I could never turn this handsome.”

p.src: Dear Great Sage! Leaving the others behind, he went straight up to the old man, bowed, and said, “Good grandfather, this humble monk offers his greetings.” Seeing how handsome and refined he was, young and nimble in body, the old man hesitated before returning his bow. Then he stroked the young monk’s head and asked with a smile, “Little monk, where have you come from?” Pilgrim replied, “We have come from the Great Tang in the Eastern Land and are journeying specially to the Western Heaven to worship the Buddha and seek the scriptures. We have just arrived here and heard you warn of a monster. My master is timid and fearful, so he sent me to ask what sort of fiend it really is that dares waylay travelers so. Please tell me all about him, grandfather, so that I may drive him out and send him packing.” The old man laughed. “You are young and know neither good nor ill, little monk, and your words do not match the facts. That fiend possesses tremendous divine powers. How dare you speak so readily of driving him away?” Pilgrim laughed. “Judging by your words, you seem intent on protecting him. You must be related to him, or else a close neighbor and sworn friend; otherwise, why magnify his might and wisdom, exalt his character, and refuse to open your heart and tell me his origins?” The old man nodded and laughed. “This monk certainly has a nimble tongue. I suppose you have traveled from place to place with your master and learned a few arts here and there—perhaps how to bind specters and goblins, ward homes, and subdue evil for people. But you have never encountered a truly savage monster.” Pilgrim asked, “How savage is he?” The old man said, “If that fiend sends a letter to Vulture Peak, five hundred arhats come to welcome him; if he dispatches a note to the Celestial Palace, each of the eleven great luminaries treats him with respect. The dragon kings of the Four Seas have been his friends, and the immortals of the Eight Grottoes often gather with him; the kings of hell in the Ten Courts call him brother, while the gods of the soil and city gods cherish him as an honored friend.”

p.src: Hearing this, the Great Sage could not restrain a hearty laugh. Taking hold of the old man, he said, “Say no more, say no more. If that fiend is merely brother and friend to my juniors and servants, he cannot be anyone very exalted. If he knew that I, this little monk, had come, he would pack up and flee before the night was out.” The old man said, “You little monk talk utter nonsense and have no proper respect. Which of those holy beings is your junior servant?” Pilgrim laughed. “To tell you the truth, I, this little monk, am originally from Water Curtain Cave on Flower-Fruit Mountain in the Kingdom of Aolai. My surname is Sun and my given name is Wukong. In former years I too was a monster and accomplished some great deeds. Once, after gathering with a host of demons and drinking several cups too many, I fell asleep. In a dream I saw two men bring a warrant and haul me off to the underworld. In a fit of rage, I wielded my gold-banded cudgel, wounded the ghostly judges, terrified the kings of hell, and nearly overturned the Hall of the Underworld. The registrar was so frightened that he fetched paper, and all ten kings of hell signed and affixed their marks, begging me to spare them a beating and willingly agreeing to become my junior servants.” On hearing this, the old man exclaimed, “Amitabha! After telling such an outrageous boast, this monk cannot expect to grow any older.” Pilgrim said, “Good sir, being as big as I am now is quite enough for me.” The old man asked, “How old are you?” Pilgrim replied, “Have a guess.” The old man said, “Seven or eight, I suppose.” Pilgrim laughed. “Ten thousand times seven or eight. I’ll show you my old face, but you must not take offense.” The old man asked, “How can you have yet another face?” Pilgrim replied, “I, this little monk, actually have seventy-two different faces.”

p.src: The old man, not understanding the trick, kept questioning him. Pilgrim wiped his face and instantly revealed his true form: baring his teeth and thrusting out his mouth, with both cheeks bright red, a tiger-skin kilt tied around his waist, and a gold-banded cudgel in his hand. Standing beneath the rocky cliff, he looked just like the living Thunder Duke. At the sight, the old man lost all color; his legs went weak and numb, and unable to stand, he fell with a thud. He scrambled up, only to stagger and stumble again. The Great Sage stepped forward and said, “Good sir, do not be needlessly alarmed. Though our faces are fierce, our hearts are kind. Don’t be afraid, don’t be afraid. Just now you kindly warned us that fiends were here. How many monsters are there in truth? Trouble yourself to tell me everything, and I will thank you properly.” The old man trembled all over and could not speak. He also pretended to be deaf and gave not a single answer.

p.src: Seeing that the old man would say no more, the Pilgrim turned and went back down the slope. The elder said, “Wukong, you are back? What did you learn?” The Pilgrim laughed. “It is nothing serious, nothing serious. There may indeed be a demon or two on the way to the Western Heaven, but the people here are timid and take them far too seriously. There is nothing to fear. I am here.” The elder said, “Did you ask him what mountain this is, what cave lies here, how many demons there are, and which road leads to Thunderclap Monastery?” Bajie said, “Master, forgive me for saying this. When it comes to competing in transformations, playing cunning tricks, and making sport of people, even three or five of us could not match Elder Brother; but when it comes to honesty, even a whole company of men like him could not match me.” The Tang Monk said, “Quite so, quite so. You are the honest one.” Bajie said, “Who knows how he blundered ahead without thinking things through? He asked a couple of questions, then came running back with nothing settled. Let old Zhu go and get the truth from him.” The Tang Monk said, “Wuneng, be careful.”

p.src: That fool tucked his rake into his sash, straightened his black robe, and minced up the slope. Calling to the old man, he said, “Greetings, grandfather.” Only after seeing the Pilgrim leave had the old man managed to struggle to his feet with the aid of his staff. He was just about to depart, still trembling, when Bajie suddenly appeared. More terrified than ever, he cried, “Merciful heavens! What evil dream did I have last night, to meet such a band of villains? Ugly as that first monk was, he still looked three parts human; but this monk has a pestle of a snout, palm-leaf-fan ears, an iron-plate face, and a bristly neck. There is not a trace of humanity in him!” Bajie laughed. “You are a joyless old grandfather, and rather fond of judging people by their looks. What sort of creature do you take me for? Ugly I may be, but I improve with looking. Gaze a while longer and I shall grow handsome.” Hearing him speak like a human, the old man had no choice but to ask, “Where do you come from?” Bajie said, “I am the Tang Monk’s second disciple. My religious name is Wuneng Bajie. The one who questioned you just now was the Pilgrim Wukong, my elder brother. Our master reproached him for offending you and failing to obtain reliable information, so he sent me especially to inquire with due respect. What mountain is this, in truth? What cave is here? What demons truly dwell inside it? Which way is the great road west? Please be so kind as to direct me.” The old man said, “Will you speak honestly?” Bajie replied, “Never in my life have I dared utter the slightest falsehood.” The old man said, “Do not pester me with slippery tricks like that monk who came before you.” Bajie said, “I am not like him.”

p.src: Leaning on his staff, the old man told Bajie, “This mountain is called the eight-hundred-li Lion-Camel Ridge. At its center stands the Lion-Camel Cave. Three demon chiefs live inside.” Bajie spat contemptuously. “You are an anxious old fellow indeed! Are a mere three demons worth all the trouble of bringing such dreadful news?” The old man said, “Are you not afraid?” Bajie replied, “To tell you the truth, of those three demons my elder brother could kill one with a single blow of his cudgel, and I could rake another to death with one stroke. We have another junior brother, who could kill the last with one blow of his demon-subduing staff. Once all three are dead, our master will pass through. What difficulty could there be?” The old man laughed. “This monk has no notion of what he faces. Those three demon chiefs possess tremendous magic powers. Of the lesser demons under their command, five thousand are stationed on the southern ridge and five thousand on the northern ridge; ten thousand guard the eastern road and ten thousand the western road; four or five thousand serve as patrols, and another ten thousand guard the gates; those who tend the fires are beyond number, as are those who gather firewood. Altogether there must be forty-seven or forty-eight thousand. These are all registered demons with names and badges, whose sole business here is eating people.”

p.src: When the fool heard this, he ran back trembling. On reaching the Tang Monk, he said nothing, but dropped his rake and squatted down to relieve himself. Seeing this, the Pilgrim shouted, “Why are you squatting there instead of reporting back?” Bajie said, “The fright made me foul myself. There is no need to say more. Let us each flee for our lives while there is still time.” The Pilgrim said, “You witless fool! I went to inquire and was not frightened in the least, yet when you go, you come back in such a senseless panic.” The elder asked, “What exactly did he say?” Bajie replied, “The old man said this mountain is the eight-hundred-li Lion-Camel Mountain. At its center stands the Lion-Camel Cave. Three old demons and forty-eight thousand lesser demons live inside, and their sole business there is eating people. If we so much as set foot along the edge of their mountain, we shall become food in their mouths. We can forget about getting through.” When Tripitaka heard this, he trembled, his hair standing on end. “Wukong, what are we to do?” The Pilgrim laughed. “Set your mind at ease, Master. It is no great matter. There may indeed be a few demons here, but the local people are timid. They exaggerate both their numbers and their size, frightening themselves with their own tales. I am here.” Bajie said, “Elder Brother, what are you saying? My inquiry was quite unlike yours. What I heard was the truth, without the slightest falsehood or error. With demons filling every mountain and valley, how can we advance?” The Pilgrim laughed. “Look at the fool! Do not frighten yourself for nothing. As for demons filling every mountain and valley, old Sun needs only sweep through with his cudgel, and by midnight I shall have wiped out every last one.” Bajie said, “Have some shame! Do not boast. It would take those demons seven or eight days merely to answer roll call. How could you possibly wipe them all out?” The Pilgrim asked, “How do you imagine I would fight them?” Bajie replied, “Even if you knocked them down, bound them up, or froze them with your body-fixing spell, you could never do it so quickly.” The Pilgrim laughed. “There is no need to seize, capture, or bind them. I shall pull at both ends of this cudgel and cry, ‘Grow long!’ and it will become some forty zhang long. Then I shall give it a shake and cry, ‘Grow thick!’ and it will become eight zhang around. One roll across the southern side of the mountain will crush five thousand to death; one roll across the northern side will crush another five thousand; and if I roll it from east to west, I warrant all forty or fifty thousand will be ground into minced flesh and bloody pulp.” Bajie said, “Elder Brother, if you mean to roll them out like dough, you might indeed finish them all by the second watch.” Sha the Monk laughed beside them. “Master, with Elder Brother possessing such powers, why should we fear those demons? Please mount your horse and let us be on our way.” Seeing them discuss their methods with such confidence, the Tang Monk had no choice but to set his mind at ease, mount his horse, and continue onward.

p.src: As they journeyed on, the old man who had brought the warning suddenly vanished. Sha Monk said, “He must be a monster himself, deliberately borrowing another’s might to frighten us with that warning.” Pilgrim said, “Don’t be hasty. Let me go and see.” The Great Sage sprang onto a lofty peak and looked all around, but found no trace of him. Turning quickly, he saw a radiant many-colored cloud in midair, so he mounted a cloud and sped after it. It was the Venus Star Lord. Drawing alongside, he seized him by the hand and repeatedly called him by his familiar name: “Li Changgeng! Li Changgeng! What a sly old idler you are! If you had something to say, why not tell me face-to-face? Why disguise yourself as a woodland elder and play such a frightening trick on old Sun?” The Star Lord hastily bowed and said, “Great Sage, forgive me for bringing the warning so late. Please do not blame me, please do not blame me. These fiends truly possess vast supernatural powers and formidable might. Only by relying on your transformations, ingenuity, and cunning may you manage to pass; but if you are careless in the least, it will truly be difficult to get through.” Pilgrim thanked him, saying, “I am grateful, truly grateful. If this place truly proves hard to pass, I ask you, venerable Star Lord, to speak to the Jade Emperor in the upper realm and borrow some heavenly troops to lend old Sun a hand.” The Star Lord said, “Certainly, certainly! Just send word, and even a hundred thousand heavenly troops will be yours.”

u.src: As they journeyed on, the old man who had brought the warning suddenly vanished.
Sha Monk said, “He must be a monster himself, deliberately borrowing another’s might to frighten us with that warning.”
Pilgrim said, “Don’t be hasty. Let me go and see.”

The Great Sage sprang onto a lofty peak and looked all around, but found no trace of him. Turning quickly, he saw a radiant many-colored cloud in midair, so he mounted a cloud and sped after it. It was the Venus Star Lord.
Drawing alongside, he seized him by the hand and repeatedly called him by his familiar name: “Li Changgeng! Li Changgeng! What a sly old idler you are!
If you had something to say, why not tell me face-to-face? Why disguise yourself as a woodland elder and play such a frightening trick on old Sun?”
The Star Lord hastily bowed and said, “Great Sage, forgive me for bringing the warning so late. Please do not blame me, please do not blame me.
These fiends truly possess vast supernatural powers and formidable might.
Only by relying on your transformations, ingenuity, and cunning may you manage to pass;
but if you are careless in the least, it will truly be difficult to get through.”
Pilgrim thanked him, saying, “I am grateful, truly grateful.
If this place truly proves hard to pass, I ask you, venerable Star Lord, to speak to the Jade Emperor in the upper realm and borrow some heavenly troops to lend old Sun a hand.”
The Star Lord said, “Certainly, certainly! Just send word, and even a hundred thousand heavenly troops will be yours.”

p.src: The Great Sage took leave of the Star Lord, lowered his cloud, and returned to Tripitaka. “That old man just now,” he said, “was actually the Venus Star Lord, who came to warn us.” The elder pressed his palms together and said, “Disciple, hurry after him and ask whether there is another road. Let us take a different way.” Pilgrim said, “There is no way around. The path through these mountains stretches for eight hundred li, and who knows how much farther it would be to go all the way around? How could we possibly detour?” Hearing this, Tripitaka could not keep tears from his eyes. “Disciple,” he said, “with hardships such as these, how are we ever to worship the Buddha?” Pilgrim said, “Don’t cry, don’t cry! The moment you cry, you become a sniveling weakling. There must have been some exaggeration in his warning; he merely wanted us to be especially vigilant. As the saying goes, ‘To give warning is to prepare against mishap.’ For now, dismount and sit here.” Bajie said, “What are we going to discuss now?” Pilgrim said, “There is nothing to discuss. Stay here and guard Master attentively, while Sha Monk keeps careful watch over the luggage and horse. Let old Sun first go up the ridge and scout about. I shall find out how many monsters there are altogether, front and rear, seize one of them, and question him thoroughly. I’ll make him write a sworn statement and draw up a register of names, investigate every one of them, old and young, order them to shut their cave gates and forbid them to block the road, and then invite Master to pass quietly through. Only then will old Sun’s skill be properly displayed.” Sha Monk merely urged him, “Be careful, be careful.” Pilgrim laughed and said, “No need to remind me. Once I set out, even if the Eastern Ocean lay in my way, I would boil a path through it; even if a mountain of silver wrapped in iron barred me, I would smash straight through its gate.”

p.src: The Great Sage gave a whistle, mounted his somersault cloud, and leaped onto a lofty peak. Clinging to vines and pulling himself through creepers, he reached a level place on the mountain and looked about. The hills were silent, with not a soul in sight. Suddenly he cried aloud, “I was wrong, I was wrong! I should never have let that old Star Lord go. So he was only trying to frighten me! What monsters could there possibly be here? If any came out to romp in the wind and amuse themselves, they would surely be brandishing spears and staffs and drilling at arms. How can there not be a single one?” As he was pondering this, he heard from behind the mountain a clanging and clattering, the rattle of a wooden clapper and bells. He turned quickly to look and saw a young fiend walking from north to south, carrying on his shoulder a banner marked “Command,” with bells hanging from his waist and a wooden clapper beating in his hand. Looking closely, he saw that the creature stood twelve feet tall. Pilgrim laughed inwardly. “He must be a dispatch runner,” he thought. “I expect he is delivering official documents and notices. Let me listen awhile and hear what he has to say.”

p.src: The Great Sage formed a hand seal, recited a spell, shook himself, and changed into a fly. He alighted softly on the fiend’s cap and cocked an ear to listen. The young fiend reached the main road, beating his clapper and shaking his bells as he chanted, “All of us who patrol the mountain must be cautious and guard against Sun the Pilgrim. He can change into a fly.” Hearing this, Pilgrim was secretly startled and suspicious. “Has this wretch seen me?” he wondered. If he has not, how does he know my name, and how does he know I can change into a fly?” In fact, the young fiend had never seen him. Somehow the demon chiefs had merely instructed him to say those words; it was only a rumor they had ordered him to repeat nonsensically. Pilgrim did not know this and instead suspected that the fiend had seen him. He was about to take out his staff and strike him, but then stopped and thought, “I remember when Bajie questioned the Star Lord, he said there were three old fiends and forty-seven or forty-eight thousand lesser fiends. Even if there were tens of thousands more little fiends like this one, they would be no cause for concern. But I do not know how powerful those three old fiends may be. Let me question him first; there will still be time enough to use force afterward.”

p.src: Now, how do you suppose the Great Sage went about questioning him? He jumped down from the fiend’s cap, settled on the top of a tree, and let the young fiend walk several paces ahead. Then he quickly turned a somersault and changed into another young fiend. Just like the first, he beat a clapper, shook bells, and carried a banner; his clothes were identical, though he stood three or five inches taller, and he chanted the same words. Catching up, he called, “You there on the road, wait for me!” The young fiend turned and asked, “Where have you come from?” Pilgrim laughed. “Well, really! Don’t you even recognize one of your own family?” The young fiend said, “There is no one like you in our household.” Pilgrim said, “How can I not be there? Take a good look and see if you recognize me.” The young fiend said, “Your face is unfamiliar. I don’t recognize you, I don’t recognize you.” Pilgrim said, “No wonder my face is unfamiliar. I tend the fires, so you have seldom had a chance to see me.” The young fiend shook his head. “No, no. Even among the brothers who tend the fires in our cave, there is no one with a pointed mouth like yours.” Pilgrim thought to himself, “I made this fine mouth of mine a little too pointed.” He immediately lowered his head, covered his mouth with his hand, rubbed it, and said, “My mouth isn’t pointed.” And indeed, it was no longer pointed. The young fiend said, “Your mouth was pointed just now. How did it become blunt merely because you rubbed it? You are a suspicious fellow, very hard to identify. You are not one of our family. We have seldom met, seldom indeed; suspicious, very suspicious! Our kings enforce the household rules very strictly: those who tend the fires do nothing but tend the fires, and those who patrol the mountain do nothing but patrol the mountain. Surely they would not have you tend the fires and also send you out to patrol the mountain?” Quick-witted Pilgrim seized on this opening and said, “You do not understand. The kings saw how well I tended the fires, so they promoted me to patrol the mountain.”

p.src: The little fiend said, “Very well. Those of us who patrol the mountain are divided into ten squads of forty, four hundred in all, each with our own age, appearance, name, and designation. His Majesty feared we might confuse the squads and make roll call difficult, so he gave each of us a badge as identification. Do you have your badge?” Wukong had copied the fiend’s appearance and manner of reporting when he transformed himself, but since he had never seen his badge, he had none upon him. The Great Sage, however, would never admit that he had none. He readily answered, “How could I have no badge? It is merely a new one I have just received. Take yours out and let me see it.” The little fiend knew nothing of the trick. He lifted his clothes and showed Wukong a gold-lacquered badge worn next to his body on a woolen cord. Wukong saw that its back bore the golden inscription “Might That Subdues All Demons,” while three proper characters on the front read “Junior Patrol-Wind.” He thought to himself, “That settles it. Every mountain patrolman must have ‘Wind’ at the end of his title.” Then he said, “Put your clothes down and walk ahead while I take out my badge to show you.” Turning around, he reached behind, plucked a fine hair from the tip of his tail, rolled it between his fingers, and cried, “Change!” It instantly became a gold-lacquered badge threaded with a green woolen cord, bearing three proper characters: “Chief Patrol-Wind.” He took it out and handed it over for inspection. The little fiend exclaimed in astonishment, “We are all called Junior Patrol-Wind. Why are you alone called some sort of ‘Chief Patrol-Wind’?” Wukong was unrivaled at contriving schemes and always knew just what to say. “You truly know nothing about it. His Majesty saw how well I tended the fires and promoted me to patrolman. He also gave me a new badge, named me Chief Patrol-Wind, and ordered me to command the forty brothers in your squad.” Hearing this, the fiend hurriedly bowed and said, “Sir, sir! You have only just been appointed, so naturally your face was unfamiliar. Forgive my offensive words.” Wukong returned the courtesy and said with a smile, “I do not blame you, but there is one thing: I expect a greeting gift. Let each man produce five taels.” The little fiend said, “Do not be impatient, sir. Wait until I meet the rest of our squad on the southern ridge, and we shall settle it all together.” Wukong said, “In that case, I shall go with you.” The little fiend truly set off in front, with the Great Sage following behind.

p.src: After a few miles, they suddenly saw a peak shaped like a writing brush. Why was it called Brush Peak? A narrow spire rose some forty or fifty feet from the mountaintop, like a brush resting upright in a stand; hence the name. When Wukong reached it, he tucked up his tail, leaped aloft, and sat on the tip of the peak. He called, “Patrol-Winds, all of you come here.” The Junior Patrol-Winds bowed below and said, “At your service, sir.” Wukong said, “Do you know why His Majesty appointed me and sent me out?” The fiends replied, “No.” Wukong said, “His Majesty wishes to eat the Tang Monk, but fears that Sun Wukong is immensely powerful and skilled in transformation. He might disguise himself as a Junior Patrol-Wind, slip in here to learn the paths, and spy out our affairs. So His Majesty promoted me to Chief Patrol-Wind and sent me to inspect your squad for impostors.” The Junior Patrol-Winds answered repeatedly, “Sir, we are all genuine.” Wukong said, “If you are genuine, do you know what powers His Majesty possesses?” A Junior Patrol-Wind replied, “I do.” Wukong said, “If you know, tell me at once. If your account agrees with what I know, you are genuine. But if you are wrong in the slightest, you are impostors, and I shall take you before His Majesty for punishment.” Seeing him seated aloft, putting on airs, shouting and browbeating them, the Junior Patrol-Wind had no choice but to tell the truth: “Our First King has vast magic and mighty powers. He once swallowed a hundred thousand celestial soldiers in a single mouthful.” At this, Wukong spat contemptuously and said, “You are an impostor.” The Junior Patrol-Wind panicked. “Honored sir, I am genuine! Why do you call me an impostor?” Wukong said, “If you are genuine, why do you speak such nonsense? How large can His Majesty’s body be, that he could swallow a hundred thousand celestial soldiers in one mouthful?” The Junior Patrol-Wind said, “So you do not know, sir. Our First King can transform himself. When he wishes to be large, he can prop up Heaven; when small, he is no bigger than a mustard seed. That year, the Queen Mother held the Peach Banquet and invited the immortals, but sent no invitation to our king. Our king intended to contest the rule of Heaven, so the Jade Emperor dispatched a hundred thousand celestial soldiers to subdue him. Our king transformed his dharma-body, opened a mouth as vast as a city gate, and tried with all his might to swallow them. The celestial troops were so terrified that they dared not engage him and shut the Southern Gate of Heaven. That is why it is said he once swallowed a hundred thousand soldiers in one mouthful.” Wukong laughed inwardly when he heard this. “If we are speaking of deeds of that sort, old Sun has done the same himself.” He then asked aloud, “What powers does the Second King possess?” The Junior Patrol-Wind said, “The Second King is thirty feet tall, with silkworm-shaped brows, phoenix eyes, a beauty’s voice, carrying-pole teeth, and a nose like a flood dragon. When he fights, one sweep of his trunk is enough—even one with an iron back and bronze body will lose both soul and spirit.” Wukong said, “A fiend who seizes people with his nose should be easy enough to capture.” Then he asked, “And what abilities does the Third King have?” The Junior Patrol-Wind said, “Our Third King is no common monster of the mortal world. His title is the Cloud-Soaring Roc of Ten Thousand Miles. When he moves, he rides the whirlwind and stirs the seas, beating northward before journeying south. He carries a treasure called the Yin-Yang Two-Qi Flask. If anyone is put inside the flask, within little more than an hour he will dissolve into liquid.”

p.src: Hearing this, Wukong was secretly alarmed. “The fiends themselves are nothing to fear, but I must guard carefully against that flask.” Then he said aloud, “Your account of the three kings’ powers was accurate and agrees with what I know. But which king is it who wishes to eat the Tang Monk?” The Junior Patrol-Wind asked, “Do you not know, sir?” Wukong shouted, “I know more than you do. But fearing that you might not know all the particulars, His Majesty ordered me to come and question you thoroughly.” The Junior Patrol-Wind said, “Our First and Second Kings have long dwelt in Lion-Camel Cave on Lion-Camel Ridge. The Third King did not live here; his original home lies some four hundred miles west of this place. There is a city there called the Kingdom of Lion-Camel. Five hundred years ago, he devoured the king of that realm and all his civil and military officials, then ate every man and woman in the city, young and old, thereby seizing the kingdom for himself. Now it is inhabited entirely by fiends. At some point he learned that the Tang court in the Eastern Land had sent a monk to the Western Heaven to fetch scriptures. It was said that this Tang Monk was a good man cultivated through ten lifetimes, and that anyone who ate a piece of his flesh would gain longevity and never grow old. But because he feared that one of the monk’s disciples, Sun Wukong, was exceedingly formidable and that he could not prevail alone, he came straight here, swore brotherhood with our two kings, and joined hearts and minds with them so that together they might capture the Tang Monk.”

p.src: Hearing this, the Pilgrim flew into a rage and said, “What an insolent fiend! I am protecting the Tang Monk on his way to attain the true fruit; how dare he scheme to eat my master?” With a furious snort, he ground his steel teeth, pulled out his iron cudgel, and leapt down from the peak. He brought the cudgel crushing down upon the little demon’s head, and, pitifully, mashed him into a lump of flesh. When he saw what he had done, he could not help feeling sorry. “Alas! He meant me well and told me all that homely gossip; how could I have finished him off with a single blow? Well, no matter. What is done is done.” Thus the Great Sage, because the road ahead was barred for his master, had no choice but to commit this deed. He took the demon’s tally from him and fastened it at his own waist, slung the command pennant across his back, hung the bell from his belt, and beat the wooden clapper in his hand. Facing the wind, he made a magic sign and recited a spell; then, with a shake of his body, he changed into the very likeness of Little Wind-Cutter. I am protecting the Tang Monk on his way to attain the true fruit; how dare he scheme to eat my master?”

With a furious snort, he ground his steel teeth, pulled out his iron cudgel, and leapt down from the peak. He brought the cudgel crushing down upon the little demon’s head, and, pitifully, mashed him into a lump of flesh.
When he saw what he had done, he could not help feeling sorry. “Alas!
He meant me well and told me all that homely gossip; how could I have finished him off with a single blow?
Well, no matter. What is done is done.”
Thus the Great Sage, because the road ahead was barred for his master, had no choice but to commit this deed.
He took the demon’s tally from him and fastened it at his own waist, slung the command pennant across his back, hung the bell from his belt, and beat the wooden clapper in his hand.
Facing the wind, he made a magic sign and recited a spell; then, with a shake of his body, he changed into the very likeness of Little Wind-Cutter.
He turned back and followed the old road straight toward the cave, intending to discover the true strength of the three old fiends.
Truly it was as follows:

p.src: He plunged deep into the mountains, following the old road. As he went, he suddenly heard men shouting and horses neighing. He raised his eyes and looked. Before the entrance to Lion-Camel Cave, tens of thousands of little demons were drawn up with spears, sabers, swords, and halberds, amid banners and streamers. The Great Sage rejoiced inwardly. “Li Changgeng’s words were indeed no falsehood—not false at all.” Their formation followed a certain system: every two hundred and fifty troops formed one great company. When he saw forty long banners of assorted colors whipping wildly in the wind, he knew there were ten thousand troops. Then he considered to himself, “I have changed into Little Wind-Cutter. Once I go inside, if the old fiend asks about my mountain patrol, I can answer according to circumstances. But if I make some slip of the tongue and he recognizes me, how shall I escape? If I try to run out, that mob guarding the gate will block me. How could I get through? To capture the demon kings inside the cave, I must first dispose of the monsters before its gate.” But how, you may ask, did he dispose of those monsters? The Great Sage thought, “That old fiend knew my name before ever meeting me. I shall rely upon that reputation and its awe-inspiring power, and tell some tall tales to see if I can frighten them. If the beings of the Middle Land truly possess the affinity and destiny to obtain the scriptures and return, then on this venture a few heroic words from me will suffice to frighten away all the monsters before the gate. But if those beings have neither affinity nor destiny and cannot obtain the true scriptures, then even if lotus flowers sprang from every word I spoke, I could not rid the western cave mouth of its fiends.” His mind questioned his mouth and his mouth questioned his mind as he weighed this plan. Beating the clapper and shaking the bell, he marched straight up to the entrance of Lion-Camel Cave. The little demons in the forward camp immediately stopped him and said, “Little Wind-Cutter, you’re back?” The Pilgrim made no reply but lowered his head and kept walking.

p.src: When he reached the second camp, more little demons caught hold of him and said, “Little Wind-Cutter, you’re back?” The Pilgrim replied, “I’m back.” The demons asked, “When you went patrolling this morning, did you happen to meet that Sun the Pilgrim?” The Pilgrim said, “I did. He is over there sharpening his great bar right now.” The demons asked fearfully, “What does he look like? What sort of bar is he sharpening?” The Pilgrim said, “As he squats beside the ravine, he already looks like a colossal road-opening god. If he stood upright, he must surely be scores of fathoms tall. In his hand he held an iron cudgel, a huge bar as thick as a bowl. He scooped up water beside the rocky cliff to sharpen it, muttering, ‘O bar, I have not brought you out to display your divine power for some time. This time, even if there are a hundred thousand demons, kill them all for me, and let me sacrifice those three fiendish chiefs to you.’ When he has sharpened it bright, he means to kill the ten thousand fiends before your gate first.” When the little demons heard this, every one of them trembled with terror, their souls scattering and their spirits taking flight. The Pilgrim added, “Gentlemen, the Tang Monk has only a few catties of flesh, and none of it will come to our share. Why should we bear the blame for them? We had better scatter and go our separate ways.” The demons all agreed. “You’re right. Let each of us go and save his own life.” These creatures were all wolves, tigers, leopards, beasts, and birds. With a single great howl, they scattered in an uproar. Those few boastful words of the Great Sage Sun proved no mere preamble; they were like the songs of Chu that scattered eight thousand troops.

p.src: The Pilgrim rejoiced inwardly. “Excellent! The old fiends are as good as dead. They fled at the mere sound of my words; how could they dare confront me face-to-face? Once inside, I had better stick to the same tale. If I change it, and one or two of those little demons turn back, go inside, and overhear me, would they not expose the whole affair?” See how, with his purpose fixed, he approached the ancient cave and boldly entered its deep gateway.
